pos: n. (East Frisian port; the Geneva of the north, refuge of the Dutch exiles, and seat of the Synod of 1571)
etymology: From Old Frisian Emutha, the mouth of the Ems; German Emden.
biblical_def: Emden was called the Geneva of the north, and it earned the name by taking people in. Under Countess Anna of Oldenburg the Polish nobleman John a Lasco organised its church in 1543 with a consistory of elders and a weekly meeting of ministers for the examination of doctrine, a model that travelled to London and back to the Netherlands; when Alva's persecution emptied the Dutch provinces of their preachers, Emden printed their books and housed their congregations. In October 1571 the first national synod of the Dutch Reformed churches met there, in exile, and adopted the Belgic Confession and the Heidelberg Catechism, laid down that no church should claim primacy over another, and set up the classes and synods that governed Dutch Protestantism thereafter. The dictionary records Emden because a church in exile wrote a constitution instead of waiting for one. “Then pleased it the apostles and elders, with the whole church, to send chosen men of their own company” (Act 15:22) is the pattern.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synod as a council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion, a presbytery as a body of elders consisting of all the pastors within a certain district, and confusion as disorder and irregular mixture.
webster_full: SYNOD, n. In church history, a council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.
PRES'BYTERY, n. A body of elders in the Christian church; a judicatory consisting of all the pastors of churches within a certain district.
CONFU'SION, n. In a general sense, a mixture of several things promiscuously; hence, disorder; irregular mixture.
DECREE, n. In theology, predetermined purpose of God; the purpose or determination of an immutable Being.
scriptures: Act 15:2

When therefore Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them, they determined that Paul and Barnabas, and certain other of them, should go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question.

Then pleased it the apostles and elders, with the whole church, to send chosen men of their own company to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas; namely, Judas surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, chief men among the brethren:
Act 16:4
And as they went through the cities, they delivered them the decrees for to keep, that were ordained of the apostles and elders which were at Jerusalem.
For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints.
corruption_summary: The Geneva of the north: a Lasco's consistory of 1543, and the first Dutch national synod, in exile, October 1571.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the independency that treats every congregation as answerable to nobody, and its mirror image, the hierarchy that makes one church the mother of the rest. Emden refused both in the same document: synods with real authority, and no church claiming primacy over another.

The principle to recover is that Christ has given the churches a connected government by assemblies of elders. A disputed question went up to an assembly rather than being settled locally: “should go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question” (Act 15:2). The assembly acted as a body with the churches: “Then pleased it the apostles and elders, with the whole church, to send chosen men of their own company” (Act 15:22). Its findings bound the congregations — “they delivered them the decrees for to keep, that were ordained of the apostles and elders” (Act 16:4) — and the reason given is the character of God: “For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints” (1Co 14:33).

pos: n. (oldest city of Holland, English Dort; host of the Synod of 1618 to 1619 and of the Statenbijbel decision)
etymology: From Middle Dutch Dordrecht, the ford on the Thure; English Dort.
biblical_def: Dordrecht was the oldest city in Holland and twice the place where the Dutch churches settled what they believed. A synod met there in 1578; and from November 1618 to May 1619 the great Synod of Dort sat in the city, with delegates from England, Scotland, Switzerland, the Palatinate, Hesse, Bremen, Emden and Geneva alongside the Dutch, examined the five articles of the Remonstrants, and set out the Canons on unconditional election, definite atonement, total depravity, effectual calling and perseverance. The same synod commissioned the Statenbijbel, the Dutch state Bible translated from the original tongues, which did for the Dutch language what Luther's did for German. The dictionary records the city as distinct from its synod, which has its own entry, because the doctrine decided there is the dictionary's own: “he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines election as the act of choosing or selecting one or more from others, predestination as the act of decreeing or foreordaining events, and a decree in theology as the predetermined purpose of God.
webster_full: ELEC'TION, n. [L. electio.] The act of choosing; choice; the act of selecting one or more from others.
PREDESTINATION, n. The act of decreeing or foreordaining events.
DECREE, n. In theology, predetermined purpose of God; the purpose or determination of an immutable Being.
FOREKNOWLEDGE, n. Knowledge of a thing before it happens; prescience.
scriptures: Eph 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
Rom 9:16
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.

Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit, and that your fruit should remain: that whatsoever ye shall ask of the Father in my name, he may give it you.

But we are bound to give thanks alway to God for you, brethren beloved of the Lord, because God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth:
corruption_summary: The oldest city of Holland, where the Synod of Dort sat from 1618 to 1619 and commissioned the Statenbijbel.
corruption_paragraphs: Arminianism is a live corruption and the most popular error in the English-speaking church. In its modern form it rarely argues the five articles; it simply assumes that God's choice follows the sinner's, that the atonement was made for all without securing any, and that grace once received may be finally lost. Dort examined those propositions against Scripture and rejected them, and the dictionary stands with the Canons.

The principle to recover is that election is God's eternal and unconditional choice, made in Christ, for His own good pleasure. The timing settles the question of ground: “According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4). Human will and effort are both excluded as the cause: “So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16). The Lord states the direction of the choosing: “Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you” (Joh 15:16). And the means are given with the end: “God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth” (2Th 2:13).

pos: n. (capital of Zeeland; seat of the English Merchant Adventurers' church and of the national synod of 1581)
etymology: From Middle Dutch Middelburg, the middle fortress, from its position on Walcheren.
biblical_def: Middelburg was the chief town of Zeeland and the port at which English Protestantism and Dutch Calvinism met. The English Merchant Adventurers had their staple there, and their congregation — a licensed English church on foreign soil — gave shelter to men the English bishops would not have: Thomas Cartwright, the leading Presbyterian of the Elizabethan church, was its minister from 1585, and Francis Johnson served it before his separatist career. The third national synod of the Dutch churches met in the city in 1581. The dictionary records Middelburg because a trading colony's chaplaincy turned into one of the formative institutions of English Puritanism: men who could not preach their convictions at home preached them to merchants abroad, and the merchants carried both the goods and the doctrine back. “How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?” (Psa 137:4) was answered, in Middelburg, by singing it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pilgrim as a wanderer, one that travels to a distance from his own country, to sojourn as to dwell in a place as a temporary resident, and captivity as subjection to a foreign power.
webster_full: PILGRIM, n. A wanderer; a traveller; particularly, one that travels to a distance from his own country.
SOJOURN, v.i. To dwell for a time; to dwell or live in a place as a temporary resident.
CAPTIVITY, n. The state of being a prisoner, or of being in the power of an enemy; subjection to a foreign power.
MERCHANT, n. A man who traffics or carries on trade with foreign countries.
scriptures: How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?
Jer 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia,
Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;
corruption_summary: Zeeland's capital, the English Merchant Adventurers' church, Cartwright's pulpit from 1585, and the national synod of 1581.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that a congregation of foreigners in a commercial colony is a chaplaincy and not a church — a service provided rather than a body with officers, discipline and a confession. Middelburg's English church had all three, and shaped a movement at home.

The principle to recover is that the people of God live as resident strangers wherever they are, and that this condition is a calling rather than an interruption of one. The lament is honest about the difficulty: “How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?” (Psa 137:4). The answer given to the exiles is to settle and to pray for the place: “seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives” (Jer 29:7). Peter addresses whole churches by that name — “to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1Pe 1:1) — and draws a moral conclusion from it: “I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts” (1Pe 2:11).

pos: n. (Dutch city and former bishopric; the Union of 1579, and the university of Gisbertus Voetius)
etymology: From Latin Ultrajectum, the ford beyond, through Middle Dutch Utrecht.
biblical_def: Utrecht was the oldest see in the Netherlands and became the headquarters of Dutch Reformed precision. The Union of Utrecht of January 1579 bound the northern provinces into the body that became the Dutch Republic; the city reformed in 1580; and from 1636 its new university had Gisbertus Voetius in the chair of theology for nearly fifty years. Voetius is the great name of the Dutch Further Reformation: a scholastic of formidable range who held that doctrine must issue in a precisely ordered life, who fought Cartesian philosophy and Cocceian covenant schemes, and whose disciples were called the precise ones by their neighbours as a term of abuse. The dictionary honours the instinct without the excesses that sometimes attended it. “See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise” (Eph 5:15) is the apostolic word for precision, and the word itself means to look carefully where one is setting his feet.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines circumspect as watchful on all sides and attentive to all circumstances, holiness as purity of moral character and freedom from sin, and godliness as piety and reverence with obedience to God's commands.
webster_full: CIRCUMSPECT, a. Watchful on all sides; cautious; attentive to all circumstances.
HOLINESS, n. 1. The state of being holy; purity or integrity of moral character; freedom from sin; sanctity.
GODLINESS, n. Piety; belief in God, with reverence and obedience to his commands; the form of godliness is the appearance without the reality.
SO'BER, a. Temperate in the use of spirituous liquors; not intoxicated; habitually temperate; grave; serious.
scriptures: Eph 5:15
See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise,
Furthermore then we beseech you, brethren, and exhort you by the Lord Jesus, that as ye have received of us how ye ought to walk and to please God, so ye would abound more and more.
Tit 2:12
Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;
Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord:
corruption_summary: The Union of 1579, and Voetius in the Utrecht chair for fifty years, the great name of the Dutch Further Reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern use of precision as an accusation, so that a Christian who orders his week, his speech and his Sabbath by rule is charged with legalism before anyone asks whether the rule is in Scripture. The Voetians were mocked for the same thing and were largely right.

The principle to recover is that sanctification is a deliberate and detailed business, pursued on purpose. The apostle asks for carefulness in the ordinary step: “See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise” (Eph 5:15). He assumes continual increase rather than a settled level: “so ye would abound more and more” (1Th 4:1). Grace itself does the teaching, and what it teaches is conduct: “denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world” (Tit 2:12). And the pursuit is not optional: “Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord” (Heb 12:14).

pos: n. (city of Holland; besieged seven months by the Spanish in 1572 and 1573, and its garrison massacred)
etymology: From Middle Dutch Haarlem, the dwelling on the sandy height, from haar and lem.
biblical_def: Haarlem endured the longest siege of the Dutch revolt. From December 1572 to July 1573 the city held out against Don Frederick of Toledo, the women of the town serving on the walls under Kenau Hasselaer; when it surrendered on terms, the terms were broken, and some two thousand of the garrison and the Reformed ministers were put to the sword or drowned in the Spaarne. The atrocity hardened the revolt and the Reformed order was established in the city within a few years. The dictionary records Haarlem because it is one of the places where the fifth seal is not a figure of speech. “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held” (Rev 6:9); and their question is the one Haarlem asked: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood” (Rev 6:10). The answer Scripture gives is that vengeance belongs to God and is certain, and that it is not ours.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines blood as, in Scripture, life itself, also slaughter, murder and the guilt of murder; vengeance as the infliction of pain in return for an injury; and to avenge as to take satisfaction for an injury by punishing the injuring party.
webster_full: BLOOD, n. [Sax. blod.] The fluid which circulates through the arteries and veins of the human body. Hence, in Scripture, life itself; also, slaughter, murder, the guilt of murder.
VENGEANCE, n. The infliction of pain on another, in return for an injury or offense; retribution.
AV'ENGE, v. To take satisfaction for an injury by punishing the injuring party.
MARTYR, n. One who suffers death in defense of the truth, particularly of the Christian faith.
scriptures: Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
Rev 6:10
And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?
Wherefore should the heathen say, Where is their God? let him be known among the heathen in our sight by the revenging of the blood of thy servants which is shed.
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
corruption_summary: The seven-month siege of 1572 and 1573, the surrender on terms, and two thousand of the garrison and ministers killed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern embarrassment at the martyrs' cry for vengeance, which is read as a failure of charity and quietly set aside. It is in the canon, it is spoken by the blessed dead, and it is answered rather than rebuked.

The principle to recover is that God will avenge the blood of His servants, that the saints may rightly ask Him to, and that they may not do it themselves. The vision is explicit about who they are: “the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held” (Rev 6:9). Their prayer is recorded without correction: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?” (Rev 6:10). The psalmist prays it too, and for God's own name's sake: “let him be known among the heathen in our sight by the revenging of the blood of thy servants” (Psa 79:10). And the prohibition on private revenge rests on that same certainty: “avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath” (Rom 12:19).

pos: n. (city of Holland; where William of Orange was assassinated in July 1584)
etymology: From Middle Dutch Delf, a ditch or delving, from the canal cut through it.
biblical_def: Delft was William of Orange's residence and the place of his death. On the tenth of July 1584 Balthasar Gerards, a Burgundian who had come to the house with a forged letter of introduction and money given him for a Bible and a pair of pistols, shot the Prince in the hall of the Prinsenhof; he was the first head of state killed with a handgun. The revolt did not collapse, as Philip had expected: the States General carried it on, and William's son Maurice finished the work. The dictionary records Delft because the assassination is one of the cleanest demonstrations in Protestant history that no man's life is at the disposal of his enemies. “My times are in thy hand” (Psa 31:15) was true of William when the shot was fired, and it is the only ground on which a man can take a position that makes him worth killing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines providence as the care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures, to appoint as to fix, to settle, to ordain by decree, and death as that state in which there is a total cessation of the vital functions.
webster_full: PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
APPOINT, v.t. To fix; to settle; to determine; to ordain by decree or decision.
DEATH, n. That state of a being, animal or vegetable, in which there is a total and permanent cessation of all the vital functions.
DECREE, n. In theology, predetermined purpose of God; the purpose or determination of an immutable Being.
scriptures: My times are in thy hand: deliver me from the hand of mine enemies, and from them that persecute me.
Job 14:5
Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months are with thee, thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass;
Act 4:28
For to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done.
Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.
corruption_summary: William of Orange shot at the Prinsenhof in July 1584, and a revolt that did not collapse with him.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern treatment of a public assassination as pure contingency — a lone man, a lucky shot, history diverted by accident — which leaves the Christian with nothing to say except that it was a shame. Scripture gives a harder and more useful account.

The principle to recover is that the length of a man's life is fixed by God and is not transferred to his enemies by their intent. The psalmist says it while being hunted: “My times are in thy hand: deliver me from the hand of mine enemies” (Psa 31:15). Job states it as a general law: “Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months are with thee, thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass” (Job 14:5). The greatest murder in history was itself within the decree: wicked men gathered “For to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done” (Act 4:28). And the death of such a man is not a loss in God's accounting: “Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints” (Psa 116:15).

pos: n. (Frisian town; seat of the university of Friesland from 1585 to 1811)
etymology: From Old Frisian Franekere, the field of the Franks or of a man named Frana.
biblical_def: Franeker was a small Frisian town with one of the best theological faculties in Europe. Its university, founded by the States of Friesland in 1585, drew an international studentry and a remarkable succession of teachers: Johannes Maccovius, the hard Polish scholastic who taught predestination without softening; William Ames, the English Puritan driven out of Cambridge who wrote on conscience and cases of conscience there; and Johannes Cocceius, whose scheme of successive covenant administrations shaped Dutch and German federal theology for two centuries. The faculty quarrelled vigorously and taught extremely well. The dictionary records Franeker because the covenant, which was its characteristic subject, is the structure of Scripture's whole dealing with men. “I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant” (Gen 17:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a covenant as a mutual agreement of two or more persons, a promise as a declaration giving a right to expect the performance of some act, and the heart as the seat of the affections and the whole inward man.
webster_full: COVENANT, n. [L. con and venio, to come together.] A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract; stipulation.
PROMISE, n. A declaration which gives to the person to whom it is made a right to expect the performance of some act.
HEART, n. The inner part of anything; the seat of the affections and passions; the will; the whole inward man.
SEED, n. The substance, animal or vegetable, which nature prepares for the reproduction and conservation of the species; offspring; progeny.
scriptures: Gen 17:7
And I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee.

But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.
Heb 8:10

For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, saith the Lord; I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts: and I will be to them a God, and they shall be to me a people:
Gal 3:17
And this I say, that the covenant, that was confirmed before of God in Christ, the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul, that it should make the promise of none effect.
corruption_summary: Friesland's university from 1585, where Maccovius, William Ames and Cocceius taught covenant and conscience.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the dispensational division of Scripture into unrelated administrations with different ways of salvation, which cuts the covenant of grace into pieces and leaves the church of the New Testament without an Old Testament. Cocceius multiplied administrations; he never multiplied covenants of grace.

The principle to recover is one covenant of grace, administered differently in different ages, with one Mediator and one promise. The Abrahamic form is perpetual and generational: “I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant” (Gen 17:7). The new administration is inward, not novel in substance: “I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts” (Jer 31:33), quoted again in “I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts” (Heb 8:10). And the later giving of the law did not cancel the earlier promise: the covenant “confirmed before of God in Christ, the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul” (Gal 3:17).

“I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts” (Jer 31:33) — Maccovius, Ames and Cocceius in its chairs.
“the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul” (Gal 3:17) — federal theology for two centuries.

pos: n. (city and province of the northern Netherlands; taken for the Republic in 1594 and reformed thereafter)
etymology: From Middle Dutch Groeningen, perhaps the people of Groni, or the green place.
biblical_def: Groningen came late. While Holland and Zeeland had been Reformed for twenty years, the city and its Ommelanden stayed under Spanish control, and the Reformation reached them only when Prince Maurice took the place by siege in July 1594; the Reduction of Groningen brought the province into the Republic, and a university followed in 1614. Francis Gomarus, who would oppose Arminius at Leiden and shape the Canons of Dort, was a native of the city, born there in 1563 while it was still Catholic. The dictionary records Groningen because the delay is instructive. God gives a city its visitation in His own time, and the twenty-year gap between Holland and Groningen was not a failure of the gospel but a difference of appointment. “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven” (Ecc 3:1), and the waiting is commanded with the promise: “though it tarry, wait for it” (Hab 2:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines time as a particular portion of duration, patience as endurance without murmuring, and longsuffering as bearing provocation for a long time and not easily provoked.
webster_full: TIME, n. 1. A particular portion or part of duration, whether past, present or future. The time was; the time has been; the time is; the time will be.
PATIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity or provocation, with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring.
LONGSUFFERING, a. Bearing injuries or provocation for a long time; patient; not easily provoked.
PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
scriptures: Ecc 3:1
To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:
Hab 2:3
For the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry.
Thou shalt arise, and have mercy upon Zion: for the time to favour her, yea, the set time, is come.
The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.
corruption_summary: The northern city taken by Maurice in 1594, reformed twenty years after Holland, and the birthplace of Gomarus.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the impatience that measures the gospel's success by the calendar, so that a region slow to receive it is written off, and a work twenty years behind its neighbours is judged to have failed. Groningen was twenty years behind Holland and produced Gomarus.

The principle to recover is that God appoints the times of visitation, and that waiting for an appointed thing is obedience rather than resignation. The seasons are fixed: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven” (Ecc 3:1). Delay is written into the promise itself: “the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry” (Hab 2:3). The mercy has its hour: “for the time to favour her, yea, the set time, is come” (Psa 102:13). And what looks like slackness is longsuffering: “The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness” (2Pe 3:9).

pos: n. (port of Holland; birthplace of Erasmus, and host of the English and Scots congregations)
etymology: From Middle Dutch Rotterdam, the dam on the Rotte.
biblical_def: Rotterdam is best known for a man who stopped short. Desiderius Erasmus was born there about 1466, edited the Greek New Testament of 1516 that put the text into the Reformers' hands, mocked the abuses of the monks and the ignorance of the clergy with unmatched skill, and then declined to break with Rome and wrote against Luther on the freedom of the will. The city itself became thoroughly Reformed and in the next century housed English and Scots congregations of exiles and merchants, including the pulpit of Hugh Peters. The dictionary records Rotterdam because its most famous son is the standing example of learning that clears the ground and will not build: scholarship without the new birth sees the corruption clearly and has no remedy for it. “the world by wisdom knew not God” (1Co 1:21), and “Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (Joh 3:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines knowledge as a clear and certain perception of that which exists, wisdom as the right use of knowledge and in Scripture true religion and piety, and regeneration as new birth by the grace of God.
webster_full: KNOWL'EDGE, n. A clear and certain perception of that which exists, or of truth and fact.
WISDOM, n. The right use or exercise of knowledge; in Scripture, true religion, godliness, piety.
REGENERA'TION, n. In theology, new birth by the grace of God; that change by which the will and natural enmity of man to God and his law are subdued.
LEARNING, n. The knowledge of principles or facts received by instruction or study; acquired knowledge or ideas in any branch of science or literature.
scriptures: For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.
Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.
Joh 3:3
Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
corruption_summary: Erasmus's birthplace, whose Greek New Testament armed the Reformers while he declined to break with Rome.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption named here is live wherever criticism substitutes for conversion. Erasmus's reform was intellectual and moral: better texts, better Latin, less superstition, kinder clergy. It was all worth having and none of it saves, and when the question came down to whether the will of fallen man is free, he took the side the dictionary names as error and Luther answered him in The Bondage of the Will.

The principle to recover is that natural wisdom cannot reach God and that the new birth is not an improvement of the old man. The method of salvation is deliberately not scholarship: “the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21). Knowledge without love inflates rather than builds: “Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth” (1Co 8:1). A man may study all his life and arrive nowhere: “Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth” (2Ti 3:7). And the requirement is absolute: “Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (Joh 3:3).

“Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth” (1Co 8:1) — and his book against Luther on the will.

pos: n. (city of Holland; the most persistent Remonstrant stronghold after the Synod of Dort)
etymology: From Middle Dutch Gouda, from the Gouwe stream and a dam.
biblical_def: Gouda was the town that would not let its Arminian preachers go. Herman Herberts had taught a doctrine of grace there since 1582 that the classis repeatedly censured and the city repeatedly protected; the magistrates backed the Remonstrant party through the whole controversy, and when the Synod of Dort deposed the Remonstrant ministers in 1619 Gouda was among the last places to conform. The dictionary records the city because the resistance was municipal rather than theological: the burghers were defending their right to appoint their own preachers as much as the preachers' doctrine, which is how error is most often maintained in a church — not by argument but by patronage. On the doctrine itself the dictionary stands with Dort: the new birth is not of the will of man, and the grace that begins the work completes it. “Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (Joh 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grace as favour and good will, perseverance as continuance in a state of grace to a state of glory, and regeneration as the change by which the natural enmity of man to God is subdued.
webster_full: GRACE, n. Favor; good will; kindness; disposition to oblige another.
PERSEVERANCE, n. Persistence in any business or enterprise undertaken; continuance in a state of grace to a state of glory.
REGENERA'TION, n. In theology, new birth by the grace of God; that change by which the will and natural enmity of man to God and his law are subdued.
ELEC'TION, n. [L. electio.] The act of choosing; choice; the act of selecting one or more from others.
scriptures: Joh 1:13
Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Php 1:6
Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:
And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.
corruption_summary: Herberts protected by the magistrates from 1582, and the city that held its Remonstrant preachers longest after Dort.
corruption_paragraphs: Arminianism is the live corruption here, and Gouda shows how it survives: by municipal patronage rather than by exegesis. The modern equivalent is a congregation or a board that keeps a man whose doctrine its own confession condemns, because he is popular, or because the right to choose him matters more than what he says. That is not liberty; it is the quiet surrender of a confession.

The principle to recover is that salvation is of God from first to last, and that the work He begins He finishes. The new birth excludes every human cause: “Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (Joh 1:13). Faith itself is given: “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8). The completion rests on the Worker and not the worked-upon: “he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Php 1:6). And the keeping is absolute: “they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand” (Joh 10:28).
